questions.tested_concept: Optic chiasm compression causing bitemporal hemianopia
questions.stem: A 46-year-old man reports bumping into doorframes on both sides for 6 months. Compression of the decussating fibers by the sellar mass shown produces which visual field defect, and which retinal fibers are injured?
options: Bitemporal hemianopia from crossing nasal retinal fiber compression
Binasal hemianopia from compression of uncrossed temporal retinal fibers
Left homonymous hemianopia from injury to the right optic tract
Right monocular blindness from compression of the right optic nerve
questions.explanation: Step 1. The diagram shows a suprasellar mass compressing the central optic chiasm, where red dashed fibers from the nasal hemiretinas cross to the contralateral optic tract. Step 2. Because nasal retinal fibers receive light from the temporal visual fields, chiasmal compression produces classic bitemporal hemianopia (shaded outer halves of both visual fields).
choice_rationales: Suprasellar growth compresses crossing nasal retinal fibers at the optic chiasm, eliminating both temporal visual fields (bitemporal hemianopia).
Uncrossed temporal retinal fibers travel laterally along the chiasm (blue lines) and carry the nasal visual fields; they are spared in central chiasmal compression.
Homonymous hemianopia results from retrochiasmal lesions (optic tract or optic radiation), not midline chiasmal compression.
Monocular blindness requires a prechiasmal lesion affecting one optic nerve anterior to the chiasm.
visual_clues: Lobulated sellar mass impinging directly on the central decussation of the optic chiasm
Interrupted red dashed fibers originating from both nasal retinas
Shaded outer (temporal) halves in both upper visual-field circles
questions.visual_target: Optic chiasm compression and bitemporal visual field loss

questions.tested_concept: Pituitary neuroendocrine tumor (PitNET) gross morphology and suprasellar compression
questions.stem: Coronal autopsy section of the brain shows a large, well-circumscribed, soft tan-pink sellar mass extending superiorly into the suprasellar cistern. Which functioning tumor type is the most common cause of this neoplasm, and which nonfunctioning type is most common overall?
options: Most common functioning: somatotroph; most common nonfunctioning: corticotroph
Functioning: lactotroph (prolactinoma); nonfunctioning: gonadotroph
Most common functioning: thyrotroph; most common nonfunctioning: lactotroph
Most common functioning: corticotroph; most common nonfunctioning: somatotroph
questions.explanation: Step 1. The coronal brain section demonstrates a classic large, soft, fleshy pituitary neuroendocrine tumor (PitNET/adenoma) expanding upward to compress the optic chiasm and elevate the floor of the third ventricle. Step 2. Lactotroph tumors (prolactinomas) are the most common functioning PitNETs, whereas gonadotroph tumors are the most common nonfunctioning PitNETs.
choice_rationales: Somatotroph tumors are the second most common functioning PitNETs, and silent corticotroph tumors are far less common than gonadotroph tumors among nonfunctioning masses.
Prolactinomas account for the majority of functioning PitNETs, while clinically nonfunctioning macroadenomas most commonly show gonadotroph (SF1) differentiation.
Thyrotroph (TSH-secreting) PitNETs are rare (~1%), and lactotroph tumors typically present with hormone excess rather than as nonfunctioning masses.
Corticotroph tumors cause Cushing disease and are less common than prolactinomas; somatotroph tumors typically cause acromegaly.
visual_clues: Large well-circumscribed tan-pink fleshy mass occupying the sellar and suprasellar midline
Upward displacement and compression of the hypothalamus and third-ventricle floor
Absence of extensive calcification or gross cystic oil-like debris
questions.visual_target: Large sellar/suprasellar PitNET on coronal gross brain section

questions.condition_overview: The WHO 2022 classification renamed pituitary adenoma to pituitary neuroendocrine tumor (PitNET) to reflect neuroendocrine lineage and occasional invasive behavior, though most remain benign and slow-growing.

questions.tested_concept: Monomorphic PitNET sheets vs variegated normal anterior pituitary and need for IHC
questions.stem: Compared with the variegated normal anterior pituitary inset (top right), the main H&E field shows uniform sheets of monomorphic round cells with bland nuclei. What is required next to determine the specific PitNET subtype?
options: PAS-Alcian blue staining to identify ciliated mucin-producing goblet cells
High-power mitotic count on H&E alone to assign secretory lineage
IHC for lineage transcription factors (PIT1, TPIT, SF1) and hormones
Congo red birefringence to separate lactotroph from somatotroph cells
questions.explanation: Step 1. Unlike the normal anterior pituitary inset (mixed acidophils, basophils, and chromophobes in small nests), a PitNET forms monotonous sheets of uniform cells with cellular monomorphism. Step 2. Because routine H&E cannot reliably identify which hormone or lineage a PitNET belongs to, immunohistochemistry (IHC) for lineage transcription factors (PIT1, TPIT, SF1) and pituitary hormones is required for subtyping.
choice_rationales: PAS-positive goblet cells and ciliated columnar epithelium characterize a benign Rathke cleft cyst rather than a PitNET.
H&E morphology and mitotic counts assess atypia or proliferation but cannot distinguish somatotroph, lactotroph, corticotroph, or gonadotroph lineages.
WHO PitNET classification relies on IHC for transcription factors (PIT1 for GH/PRL/TSH, TPIT for ACTH, SF1 for FSH/LH) plus hormone stains and Ki-67 proliferation index.
Congo red identifies amyloid deposition rather than pituitary endocrine lineage.
visual_clues: Main field showing diffuse sheets of uniform, monomorphic cells with round bland nuclei
Loss of the normal nested acinar architecture seen in the upper-right inset
Inset demonstrating normal mixed pink acidophils, purple basophils, and pale chromophobes
questions.visual_target: Monomorphic PitNET histology contrasted with normal variegated anterior pituitary

questions.condition_overview: Normal anterior pituitary histology contains a mosaic of acidophils (GH, PRL), basophils (ACTH, TSH, FSH, LH), and chromophobes arranged in tight acini. Cellular uniformity (monomorphism) is a hallmark of neoplastic PitNET proliferation.

questions.tested_concept: Reticulin stain distinguishing pituitary hyperplasia from PitNET neoplasia
questions.stem: Both biopsy panels are stained with reticulin. Which interpretation accurately distinguishes Panel A from Panel B?
options: Panel A shows normal posterior pituitary Herring bodies; Panel B shows anterior pituitary ischemic necrosis
Panel A shows disrupted reticulin loss (PitNET); Panel B shows intact acinar architecture (hyperplasia)
Panel A shows wet keratin nodules (craniopharyngioma); Panel B shows lymphocytic infiltration (hypophysitis)
Panel A: intact expanded acinar reticulin (hyperplasia); Panel B: lost reticulin (PitNET)
questions.explanation: Step 1. Reticulin stains the dark basement-membrane fiber network surrounding normal anterior pituitary acini. Step 2. Panel A preserves a continuous (though expanded) acinar reticulin meshwork typical of pituitary hyperplasia, whereas Panel B demonstrates breakdown and loss of the reticulin network—the diagnostic hallmark of a pituitary neuroendocrine tumor (neoplasia).
choice_rationales: Herring bodies are neurosecretory axonal dilatations in the posterior pituitary, and ischemic necrosis shows ghost cells rather than intact vs. disrupted acinar reticulin.
This reverses the two panels: the continuous dark rings outlining nests are in Panel A, while the fragmented, lost meshwork is in Panel B.
Wet keratin and lymphocytic infiltrates are H&E findings in craniopharyngioma and lymphocytic hypophysitis, not reticulin basement-membrane patterns.
Intact, widened acinar outlines on reticulin stain identify hyperplasia (Panel A), whereas breakdown and disappearance of the reticulin framework confirm neoplasia/PitNET (Panel B).
visual_clues: Panel A: continuous dark reticulin rings outlining expanded, intact cellular acini
Panel B: fragmented, sparse, and largely absent reticulin fibers across sheets of cells
Green counterstain highlighting cellular parenchyma between black argyrophilic fibers
questions.visual_target: Reticulin framework preservation (A) versus disruption (B)

questions.tested_concept: Radiologic classification of PitNET microadenoma (<1 cm) vs macroadenoma (≥1 cm)
questions.stem: Coronal contrast-enhanced T1-weighted MRIs from two patients with sellar lesions (yellow arrowheads) are shown side by side. What size threshold separates the lesion in Panel A from the lesion in Panel B?
options: Panel A is a microadenoma (<1 cm); Panel B is a macroadenoma (≥1 cm)
Panel A is a microadenoma (<2 cm); Panel B is a macroadenoma (≥2 cm)
Panel A is an empty sella (<0.5 cm); Panel B is a Rathke cleft cyst (≥0.5 cm)
Panel A is a macroadenoma (≥1 cm); Panel B is a microadenoma (<1 cm)
questions.explanation: Step 1. Panel A shows a small, focal, hypoenhancing intrasellar lesion confined well within the sella turcica, whereas Panel B shows a larger sellar mass expanding laterally toward the cavernous sinus and superiorly toward the suprasellar cistern. Step 2. Radiologically, PitNETs are classified as microadenomas when <1 cm (<10 mm) in diameter (Panel A) and macroadenomas when ≥1 cm (≥10 mm) (Panel B).
choice_rationales: The standard radiologic cutoff separating pituitary microadenomas (<1 cm, Panel A) from macroadenomas (≥1 cm, Panel B) is 1 cm (10 mm).
The threshold is 1 cm, not 2 cm; lesions between 1 and 2 cm are already classified as macroadenomas and can compress adjacent structures.
Empty sella shows CSF filling the sella with a flattened gland along the floor rather than a focal enhancing/hypoenhancing sellar mass.
This reverses the two panels: the smaller intrasellar lesion is in Panel A and the larger expanding mass is in Panel B.
visual_clues: Panel A: small focal hypoenhancing intrasellar lesion (<1 cm) with an intact midline stalk
Panel B: larger mass (≥1 cm) expanding the sella and abutting the cavernous internal carotid artery
Yellow arrowheads marking the pituitary lesions on coronal post-contrast T1 MRI

questions.tested_concept: Adamantinomatous (CTNNB1, wet keratin) vs papillary (BRAF p.V600E) craniopharyngioma
questions.stem: Resection specimens from two suprasellar Rathke pouch–derived tumors are shown side by side. Which pairing of subtype, typical age group, and driver mutation matches Panel A and Panel B?
options: Panel A: papillary (adults, BRAF p.V600E); Panel B: adamantinomatous (children, CTNNB1/β-catenin)
Panel A: adamantinomatous (children, CTNNB1); Panel B: papillary (adults, BRAF p.V600E)
Panel A: Rathke cleft cyst (infants, no mutation); Panel B: lactotroph PitNET (adults, PIT1)
Panel A: adamantinomatous (adults, BRAF p.V600E); Panel B: papillary (children, CTNNB1/β-catenin)
questions.explanation: Step 1. Panel A displays prominent eosinophilic 'wet keratin' nodules, peripheral nuclear palisading, and loose stellate reticulum—classic hallmarks of adamantinomatous craniopharyngioma. Panel B displays solid, well-differentiated non-keratinizing squamous epithelium draping over fibrovascular cores (cauliflower-like papillae) without wet keratin—classic papillary craniopharyngioma. Step 2. Adamantinomatous craniopharyngioma predominantly affects children and carries CTNNB1 (β-catenin) mutations, whereas papillary craniopharyngioma occurs almost exclusively in adults and carries BRAF p.V600E mutations.
choice_rationales: This swaps the two histology panels: eosinophilic wet keratin whorls are in Panel A, whereas papillary fibrovascular cores are in Panel B.

Panel A shows wet keratin and palisading of pediatric-predominant CTNNB1-mutant adamantinomatous craniopharyngioma, while Panel B shows non-keratinizing squamous papillae of adult BRAF p.V600E papillary craniopharyngioma.
Rathke cleft cysts are lined by simple ciliated cuboidal/columnar epithelium with goblet cells, and PitNETs show monotonous neuroendocrine sheets rather than squamous papillae.
This swaps the age groups and driver mutations: CTNNB1 drives adamantinomatous tumors (bimodal, mainly children) and BRAF p.V600E drives adult papillary tumors.
visual_clues: Panel A: bright pink anucleate 'wet keratin' nodules surrounded by palisading basal epithelium and loose stellate reticulum
Panel B: papillary projections of mature non-keratinizing stratified squamous epithelium covering fibrovascular cores
Absence of wet keratin or calcification in Panel B
questions.visual_target: Adamantinomatous (A) vs. papillary (B) craniopharyngioma histology

Papillary craniopharyngiomas are typically solid, non-calcified, well-circumscribed, and amenable to BRAF-targeted therapy.

questions.tested_concept: Pituitary apoplexy acute hemorrhage, cavernous sinus ophthalmoplegia, and urgent management
questions.stem: A 54-year-old man with a known pituitary macroadenoma develops a sudden thunderclap 'worst headache of his life,' bilateral diplopia (label 3), and acute visual loss (label 2). What acute mechanism is illustrated, and what is the most urgent initial medical and surgical management?
options: Slow CSF herniation through the diaphragma sellae; elective observation with repeat MRI in 1 year
Autoimmune lymphocytic infiltration of the stalk; outpatient oral levothyroxine monotherapy
Acute PitNET hemorrhage/infarction; urgent IV glucocorticoids and surgical decompression
Postpartum ischemic infarction of the anterior lobe; high-dose oral cabergoline therapy
questions.explanation: Step 1. The diagram depicts acute hemorrhage/infarction within a sellar tumor expanding superiorly into the optic chiasm (2) and third ventricle (1, obstructive hydrocephalus) and laterally into both cavernous sinuses (3, CN III/IV/VI ophthalmoplegia). Step 2. Pituitary apoplexy is a neuroendocrine emergency requiring immediate IV glucocorticoid replacement (to prevent fatal adrenal crisis) and urgent transsphenoidal surgical decompression for neuro-ophthalmic deficits.
choice_rationales: Empty sella is a chronic CSF herniation that rarely causes sudden thunderclap headache or acute bilateral cavernous sinus ophthalmoplegia.
Lymphocytic hypophysitis presents subacutely (often peripartum or with CTLA-4 inhibitors) and giving levothyroxine alone without cortisol risks precipitating adrenal crisis.
Sudden thunderclap headache (89%) with ophthalmoplegia (78%) and visual loss (52%) defines pituitary apoplexy, which requires emergent IV hydrocortisone and urgent transsphenoidal decompression.
Sheehan syndrome occurs after severe postpartum hemorrhage rather than hemorrhage into a preexisting macroadenoma, and cabergoline does not relieve acute apoplexy compression.
visual_clues: Central hemorrhagic crimson sellar mass expanding acutely in all four directions
Lateral arrows invading bilateral cavernous sinuses containing cranial nerves (label 3)
Superior arrows compressing the optic chiasm (label 2) and third ventricle (label 1)
questions.visual_target: Directional mass effects of acute pituitary apoplexy

questions.tested_concept: Rathke cleft cyst ciliated columnar epithelium with mucin-producing goblet cells
questions.stem: A 34-year-old woman undergoes transsphenoidal drainage of a benign, non-calcified, mucoid intrasellar cyst. Histology shows a single layer of ciliated columnar epithelium (panel a) with PAS-positive mucin-producing goblet cells (panel c). What is the diagnosis and embryologic origin?
options: Ectopic posterior pituitary arising from arrested migration of hypothalamic magnocellular axons
Adamantinomatous craniopharyngioma arising from the neuroectodermal infundibulum
Pituitary neuroendocrine tumor arising from monomorphic PIT1-positive acidophils
Rathke cleft cyst arising from an embryologic remnant of Rathke pouch (oral ectoderm)
questions.explanation: Step 1. The biopsy shows benign, single-layered ciliated cuboidal-to-columnar epithelium (a) interspersed with PAS-positive mucin-filled goblet cells (c), with no wet keratin or neoplastic sheets. Step 2. These features are pathognomonic for a Rathke cleft cyst, a benign developmental remnant of the oral ectodermal Rathke pouch.
choice_rationales: Ectopic posterior pituitary appears as a T1-bright neurohypophyseal nodule at the median eminence rather than a mucin-filled epithelial cyst.

Adamantinomatous craniopharyngioma also arises from Rathke pouch remnants (not neuroectoderm) but features stratified squamous epithelium, peripheral palisading, and wet keratin rather than simple ciliated goblet-cell epithelium.
PitNETs consist of solid sheets of monomorphic neuroendocrine cells without ciliated epithelium or mucinous goblet cells.
Simple ciliated columnar/cuboidal epithelium with PAS-positive goblet cells lining a mucoid sellar cyst defines a benign Rathke cleft cyst derived from Rathke pouch.
visual_clues: Panel (a): thin single layer of simple ciliated columnar epithelium (arrow) over fibrous wall
Panel (c): plump purple PAS-positive mucin-producing goblet cells (arrow) lining the cyst lumen
Complete absence of wet keratin, peripheral palisading, or cellular atypia
questions.visual_target: Ciliated columnar epithelium and PAS-positive goblet cells of a Rathke cleft cyst

questions.tested_concept: Septo-optic dysplasia diagnostic triad and most common hormone deficiency
questions.stem: An infant evaluated for nystagmus and poor visual tracking undergoes brain MRI (coronal left, sagittal right), demonstrating fused squared-off frontal horns without a midline septum pellucidum, a hypoplastic optic chiasm (OC), and a small anterior pituitary (AP). What is the diagnosis, and which pituitary hormone is most commonly deficient?
options: Septo-optic dysplasia; growth hormone (GH) deficiency
Alobar holoprosencephaly; isolated prolactin excess
Kallmann syndrome; isolated vasopressin (ADH) deficiency
Empty sella syndrome; isolated ACTH excess
questions.explanation: Step 1. The MRI demonstrates classic features of septo-optic dysplasia (de Morsier syndrome): absent septum pellucidum (box-like fused lateral ventricles), optic nerve/chiasm hypoplasia, and pituitary hypoplasia. Step 2. Diagnosis requires ≥2 of these three triad features; visual impairment is usually the first sign, and GH deficiency is the most common endocrine deficit.
choice_rationales: Absent septum pellucidum, optic chiasm hypoplasia, and pituitary hypoplasia fulfill the diagnostic triad of septo-optic dysplasia, in which GH is the most frequent hormonal deficiency.

Alobar holoprosencephaly produces a single monoventricle with complete failure of forebrain cleavage and severe midline facial defects (cyclopia/proboscis), not isolated absence of the septum pellucidum.
Kallmann syndrome presents with anosmia and hypogonadotropic hypogonadism from failed GnRH neuron migration, without absent septum pellucidum or optic nerve hypoplasia.
Empty sella syndrome shows CSF filling the sella in adults (commonly obese females) and does not cause congenital absent septum pellucidum or optic chiasm hypoplasia.
visual_clues: Coronal MRI (left): absent midline septum pellucidum producing a squared-off single anterior ventricular roof
Sagittal MRI (right): hypoplastic anterior pituitary (AP) and thin optic chiasm (OC)
Intact corpus callosum (CC) separating septo-optic dysplasia from severe holoprosencephaly
questions.visual_target: Absent septum pellucidum, optic chiasm hypoplasia, and pituitary hypoplasia on MRI

questions.tested_concept: Alobar holoprosencephaly failure of prosencephalon cleavage
questions.stem: A newborn presents with the severe midline craniofacial anomaly (Panel B) and axial brain MRI (Panel A) showing a single horseshoe-shaped monoventricle with fused thalami and no interhemispheric fissure. Failure of cleavage of which embryonic brain vesicle causes this most severe subtype?
options: Rhombencephalon (hindbrain), producing lobar holoprosencephaly
Prosencephalon (forebrain), producing alobar holoprosencephaly
Mesencephalon (midbrain), producing septo-optic dysplasia
Oral ectodermal Rathke pouch, producing pituitary stalk interruption
questions.explanation: Step 1. Panel A shows complete absence of the interhemispheric fissure with a single monoventricle (red arrow) and fused midline deep gray nuclei (blue arrow), paired in Panel B with cyclopia/synophthalmia and a supraorbital proboscis. Step 2. This is alobar holoprosencephaly, the most severe form of failed midline cleavage of the embryonic prosencephalon (forebrain).
choice_rationales: Holoprosencephaly is a forebrain (prosencephalon) defect rather than a hindbrain defect, and lobar HPE is a milder subtype with mostly separated hemispheres.

Alobar holoprosencephaly represents complete failure of embryonic prosencephalon cleavage into two cerebral hemispheres, accompanied by the most severe midline facial defects and hypothalamic-pituitary dysfunction.
Septo-optic dysplasia involves midline optic/septal structures without a single monoventricle or cyclopia, and does not stem from mesencephalic failure.
Rathke pouch forms the anterior pituitary rather than the cerebral hemispheres and facial midline.
visual_clues: Panel A (MRI): large single dorsal monoventricle (red arrow) with fused midline thalami (blue arrow) and absent interhemispheric fissure
Panel B (Clinical photo): single central fused orbit (red arrow) beneath a midline proboscis (blue arrow)
Classic 'face predicts the brain' severity correlation in alobar holoprosencephaly

questions.tested_concept: Pituitary stalk interruption syndrome with ectopic posterior pituitary bright spot
questions.stem: A 7-year-old boy with proportionate short stature undergoes unenhanced sagittal T1-weighted MRI. The normal posterior pituitary bright spot is absent from the sella (red arrow shows a hypoplastic anterior gland), and a high-T1 nodule sits superiorly at the median eminence (blue arrow). What is this finding?
options: Craniopharyngioma with dystrophic suprasellar calcification
Empty sella syndrome caused by idiopathic intracranial hypertension
Ectopic posterior pituitary (pituitary stalk interruption syndrome)
Pituitary macroadenoma with acute intratumoral hemorrhage
questions.explanation: Step 1. Normally, neurosecretory granules in the posterior pituitary produce a bright T1 hyperintense spot inside the posterior sella turcica. Step 2. Absence of the intrasellar bright spot paired with an ectopic T1-bright nodule at the median eminence/hypothalamus (blue arrow), a thin/absent stalk, and a small anterior pituitary (red arrow) is the classic MRI triad of pituitary stalk interruption syndrome (ectopic posterior pituitary).
choice_rationales: Craniopharyngiomas present as larger cystic-solid suprasellar masses with calcifications rather than a tiny discrete ectopic T1-bright posterior pituitary dot.
Empty sella shows a CSF-filled sella flattening the pituitary along the floor without an ectopic bright neurohypophyseal nodule at the median eminence.
The displaced T1-hyperintense neurohypophyseal bright spot at the median eminence with anterior pituitary hypoplasia defines ectopic posterior pituitary / stalk interruption syndrome.
Pituitary apoplexy produces a large hemorrhagic sellar mass causing acute headache and ophthalmoplegia, not a hypoplastic intrasellar gland.
visual_clues: Blue arrow: discrete T1-hyperintense bright nodule located superiorly at the median eminence
Red arrow: markedly hypoplastic anterior pituitary inside a small sella turcica
Absent normal posterior pituitary bright spot within the sella and attenuated stalk
questions.visual_target: Ectopic T1-bright posterior pituitary nodule and hypoplastic anterior pituitary

questions.tested_concept: Lymphocytic hypophysitis autoimmune infiltrate, pregnancy/CTLA-4 link, and MRI mimic
questions.stem: A 31-year-old woman in her third trimester develops headache and hypocortisolism with a symmetrically thickened pituitary stalk on MRI mimicking a PitNET. Biopsy shows dense sheets of small mature lymphocytes and plasma cells effacing anterior pituitary acini. Which clinical association is most characteristic of this condition?
options: Rathke cleft cyst rupture provoking a foreign-body keratin granuloma
Sheehan syndrome triggered by severe obstetric hemorrhage and ischemic coagulative necrosis
Pituitary neuroendocrine tumor driven by clonal proliferation of monomorphic acidophils
Autoimmune lymphocytic hypophysitis linked to pregnancy, Hashimoto thyroiditis, or CTLA-4 blockade
questions.explanation: Step 1. The H&E biopsy shows diffuse, dense lymphoplasmacytic infiltration destroying residual pink anterior pituitary acini—classic autoimmune lymphocytic hypophysitis. Step 2. It predominantly affects women (F:M ~6:1), typically during late pregnancy or postpartum, is strongly associated with other autoimmune endocrinopathies (like Hashimoto thyroiditis) and immune checkpoint inhibitors (especially CTLA-4 blockade), and mimics a PitNET on MRI.
choice_rationales: Rathke cleft cyst histology shows ciliated columnar epithelium and goblet cells rather than autoimmune lymphoplasmacytic effacement.
Sheehan syndrome causes bland ischemic coagulative necrosis following massive postpartum hemorrhage rather than a dense autoimmune lymphocytic infiltrate.
PitNETs consist of uniform sheets of neoplastic endocrine cells without dense inflammatory lymphocytic destruction.
Dense lymphoplasmacytic infiltration in a peripartum woman with stalk thickening defines lymphocytic hypophysitis, which associates with Hashimoto thyroiditis and CTLA-4 inhibitors.
visual_clues: Dense infiltrate of small dark round lymphocytes and plasma cells filling the anterior pituitary
Scattered residual islands of bright pink anterior pituitary endocrine cells trapped within inflammation
Absence of monomorphic adenoma sheets or ischemic coagulative necrosis
questions.visual_target: Dense lymphoplasmacytic infiltrate destroying anterior pituitary parenchyma

questions.stem: Comparing an earlier portrait (right) with a later portrait (left) of the same adult woman reveals progressive coarsening of facial features, broadened nose, thickened lips, and prominent brow/jaw. Why is a single random GH level unreliable for diagnosis, and what is the correct screening and confirmatory sequence?
options: GH has a 20-hour half-life; screen with random GH, then confirm with an insulin-induced hypoglycemia test
GH is pulsatile; screen with IGF-1, then confirm with failed GH suppression on OGTT
GH is tonically inhibited by dopamine; screen with serum prolactin, then confirm with a water deprivation test
GH rises only during pregnancy; screen with urine free cortisol, then confirm with low-dose dexamethasone
questions.explanation: Step 1. The longitudinal portraits show classic adult-onset acromegaly (post-epiphyseal fusion), with progressive soft-tissue and craniofacial bone enlargement from chronic GH/IGF-1 excess. Step 2. Because pituitary GH secretion is pulsatile, a single random GH level is uninformative; diagnosis starts with measuring stable serum IGF-1 and is confirmed by failure of GH to suppress during an oral glucose tolerance test (OGTT).
choice_rationales: IGF-1—not GH—has the ~20-hour half-life; insulin-induced hypoglycemia tests for GH or ACTH deficiency rather than GH excess.
Pulsatile GH fluctuates widely throughout the day, so elevated serum IGF-1 is the best initial screen and non-suppressible GH during an OGTT confirms autonomous somatotroph excess.
Water deprivation tests evaluate diabetes insipidus, and prolactin screening evaluates lactotroph excess rather than acromegaly.
Urine free cortisol and dexamethasone suppression evaluate Cushing syndrome (hypercortisolism), not somatotroph GH excess.

Coarsening of facial soft tissues and deepening nasolabial folds over years
Adult onset after epiphyseal plate closure (acral/facial growth without tall stature)

questions.tested_concept: Central vs nephrogenic diabetes insipidus sites, causes, and desmopressin response
questions.stem: A patient with polyuria (>5 L/day), polydipsia, serum Na⁺ 150 mEq/L, and urine osmolality 120 mOsm/kg undergoes a water deprivation test followed by desmopressin (DDAVP). Urine osmolality remains flat during deprivation but rises by >50% after desmopressin. Which site in the diagram is defective, and what is a classic cause of Site 2?
options: Site 2 (gestational DI: placental vasopressinase); Site 1 (nephrogenic DI) responds to fluid restriction alone
Site 2 (nephrogenic DI: renal ADH unresponsiveness); Site 1 (central DI) is classically caused by lithium
Site 1 (SIAD: excess ADH secretion); Site 2 (primary polydipsia) is classically caused by pituitary surgery
Site 1 (central DI: ADH deficiency); Site 2 (nephrogenic DI) is classically caused by lithium
questions.explanation: Step 1. Polyuria with hypernatremia and severely dilute urine (<200 mOsm/kg) confirms diabetes insipidus; a >50% jump in urine osmolality after desmopressin localizes the defect to Site 1 (central DI—deficient hypothalamic/posterior pituitary ADH secretion, where kidneys remain responsive to exogenous ADH). Step 2. Site 2 represents nephrogenic DI (ADH-unresponsive renal collecting ducts), classically caused by lithium or intrinsic renal disease.
choice_rationales: Gestational DI results from placental vasopressinase degrading circulating AVP (and responds to vasopressinase-resistant desmopressin), not Site 2 renal resistance.
Nephrogenic DI (Site 2) fails to concentrate urine after desmopressin because renal V₂ receptors/aquaporins are unresponsive, and lithium causes nephrogenic—not central—DI.
SIAD produces euvolemic hyponatremia with concentrated urine (>300 mOsm/kg), the exact opposite of hypernatremic dilute polyuria.
Desmopressin restores collecting-duct water reabsorption in Site 1 (central DI from tumors, trauma, or surgery), whereas Site 2 (nephrogenic DI) is ADH-resistant and classically triggered by lithium.
visual_clues: Site 1 located at the hypothalamic supraoptic/paraventricular nuclei, stalk, and posterior pituitary
Site 2 located at the kidney receiving the hormonal arrow from the posterior pituitary
Downstream outcome showing loss of water leading to polyuria, polydipsia, and dehydration
questions.visual_target: Anatomic separation of central (Site 1) and nephrogenic (Site 2) diabetes insipidus

questions.tested_concept: SIAD pathophysiology, V2 receptor aquaporin-2 insertion, and vaptan selective water diuresis
questions.stem: A 63-year-old man with small-cell lung cancer has euvolemic hyponatremia (Na⁺ 124 mEq/L), plasma osmolality 258 mOsm/kg, and urine osmolality 480 mOsm/kg. In the collecting duct principal cell diagram shown, what receptor does the green drug block, and what channel's apical insertion is prevented?
options: V₂ receptor blockade preventing AQP2 insertion, causing selective free-water diuresis
V₁a receptor blockade preventing Na⁺/K⁺-ATPase activation, producing natriuresis and hypotension
Mineralocorticoid receptor blockade preventing ENaC insertion, producing potassium-sparing diuresis
V₂ receptor agonism accelerating aquaporin-2 (AQP2) insertion, concentrating the urine further
questions.explanation: Step 1. Euvolemic hyponatremia (<130 mEq/L) with low plasma osmolality (<270 mOsm/kg) and inappropriately concentrated urine (>300 mOsm/kg) defines SIAD (excess ADH action). Step 2. Vaptans (green drug) competitively block basolateral V₂ receptors on collecting duct principal cells, preventing vesicular aquaporin-2 (AQP2) insertion into the apical membrane and inducing selective free-water diuresis (aquaresis) that raises plasma osmolality.
choice_rationales: Vaptans antagonize principal-cell V₂ receptors to block AQP2 trafficking, increasing free-water excretion and normalizing serum Na⁺ in SIAD.
V₁a receptors mediate vascular smooth muscle vasoconstriction rather than collecting duct AQP2 water channel insertion.
Mineralocorticoid receptor antagonists (e.g., spironolactone) block aldosterone-driven ENaC Na⁺ reabsorption rather than ADH-driven AQP2 water channels.
V₂ agonists (like desmopressin) treat central DI and would worsen hyponatremia in SIAD.
visual_clues: Basolateral receptor on a collecting duct principal cell blocked by the green antagonist (red X)
Intracellular vesicle holding water channels blocked from fusing with the apical tubular lumen
Outcome arrows showing increased plasma osmolality and increased dilute urine output

questions.tested_concept: Sheehan syndrome postpartum anterior pituitary ischemic necrosis sparing posterior lobe
questions.stem: A 32-year-old woman who required emergency transfusion for massive obstetric bleeding cannot breastfeed after delivery and later develops amenorrhea, fatigue, and cold intolerance. Based on the pathogenesis diagram shown, why is posterior pituitary function (ADH) typically spared?
options: The posterior pituitary undergoes lactotroph hyperplasia during pregnancy that protects it from ischemia
Direct arterial perfusion protects the posterior lobe, while the anterior lobe relies on portal veins
Oxytocin and ADH are synthesized inside the maternal adrenal cortex and bypass the sella turcica
Anti-pituitary autoantibodies selectively destroy posterior pituicytes only after 10 years
questions.explanation: Step 1. During pregnancy, estrogen-driven lactotroph hyperplasia enlarges the anterior pituitary, increasing its metabolic demand and compressing local vessels; severe postpartum hemorrhage (Trigger) precipitates acute ischemic necrosis of the anterior lobe (Sheehan syndrome), presenting first with failure to lactate (PRL deficiency) and evolving into panhypopituitarism. Step 2. The posterior pituitary is typically spared because it has its own direct arterial supply (inferior hypophyseal artery) rather than relying solely on the low-pressure hypophyseal portal system.
choice_rationales: Lactotroph hyperplasia occurs in the anterior pituitary (making it more—not less—vulnerable to hypotension), not in the posterior pituitary.
Direct arterial perfusion protects the posterior pituitary during hypovolemic shock, whereas the enlarged, portal-fed anterior pituitary suffers ischemic infarction (Sheehan syndrome).
ADH and oxytocin are synthesized in hypothalamic magnocellular nuclei, not the adrenal cortex.
Posterior lobe sparing is an anatomic vascular phenomenon rather than delayed autoimmune targeting.
visual_clues: Top panels showing marked anterior pituitary enlargement during pregnancy compressing sellar vasculature
Left trigger box (severe postpartum hemorrhage) precipitating ischemia and anterior lobe necrosis
Downstream multi-organ deficiencies affecting mammary gland (PRL), thyroid (TSH), adrenal (ACTH), ovary (FSH/LH), and muscle/bone (GH)

questions.stem: A 17-year-old boy has delayed puberty, small testes, low testosterone, low LH/FSH, and complete inability to smell coffee or peppermint. In the developmental pathway shown, the upper red X blocks migration of GnRH neurons from which embryonic structure?

Oral ectodermal Rathke pouch, causing isolated growth hormone deficiency and short stature
Olfactory placode, causing hypogonadotropic hypogonadism with anosmia (Kallmann)
Third-ventricle floor, causing septo-optic dysplasia with absent septum pellucidum

The diagram shows a developmental block (top red X) preventing immature neurons from migrating into the hypothalamus to become GnRH neurons, cascading into absent portal GnRH, absent pituitary FSHβ/LHβ, and hypogonadism. Step 2. Because GnRH neurons normally migrate along olfactory axons from the embryonic olfactory (nasal) placode, failure of this migration produces Kallmann syndrome: hypogonadotropic hypogonadism plus anosmia/hyposmia.

Rathke pouch forms the anterior pituitary gland itself rather than the migratory path of hypothalamic GnRH neurons.
Failed migration of GnRH-producing neurons from the olfactory (nasal) placode into the hypothalamus links absent smell (anosmia) with low GnRH, LH, FSH, and sex steroids in Kallmann syndrome.
Septo-optic dysplasia causes optic nerve hypoplasia, absent septum pellucidum, and GH deficiency rather than isolated anosmia with hypogonadotropic hypogonadism.

questions.stem: A suprasellar craniopharyngioma injures specific hypothalamic nuclei labeled A–D in the diagram. Which lesion-to-syndrome pairing is correct?
options: Lesion at C (ventromedial nucleus) → anorexia/emaciation; lesion at A (paraventricular nucleus) → acromegaly
Lesion at A (paraventricular nucleus) → hyperphagia; lesion at C (ventromedial nucleus) → diabetes insipidus
Lesion at B (supraoptic nucleus) → circadian rhythm loss; lesion at D (arcuate nucleus) → poikilothermia
C (ventromedial) → hyperphagia/obesity; D (arcuate) → hyperprolactinemia

On the diagram, A is the paraventricular nucleus and B is the supraoptic nucleus (ADH/oxytocin synthesis → lesions cause central diabetes insipidus); C is the ventromedial nucleus (satiety center) and D is the arcuate nucleus (tuberoinfundibular dopamine + POMC/AgRP neurons). Circadian rhythm is controlled by the suprachiasmatic nucleus (just above the optic chiasm), and poikilothermia results from posterior hypothalamic nucleus injury.
Ventromedial nucleus (C) destruction causes hyperphagia/obesity (satiety loss), and arcuate nucleus (D) destruction eliminates dopamine inhibition of lactotropes, raising prolactin.

questions.tested_concept: Macroprolactinoma (>200 ng/mL) first-line dopamine agonist management
questions.stem: A 36-year-old woman with amenorrhea, galactorrhea, and mild bitemporal visual blurring has a serum prolactin of 640 ng/mL. Sagittal MRI demonstrates a 2.2 cm well-circumscribed sellar/suprasellar mass. What is the most appropriate first-line treatment?
options: Immediate transsphenoidal surgical resection, as medical therapy is ineffective for macroadenomas
Oral dopamine agonist (cabergoline or bromocriptine) to suppress prolactin and shrink the tumor
High-dose somatostatin analog (octreotide) plus pegvisomant
Observation alone because prolactin >200 ng/mL reflects benign stalk compression
questions.explanation: Step 1. A 2.2 cm sellar macroadenoma (>1 cm) paired with a markedly elevated serum prolactin (>200 ng/mL) confirms a macroprolactinoma rather than stalk-effect hyperprolactinemia (which is usually <200 ng/mL). Step 2. Unlike other PitNETs where surgery is first-line, first-line treatment for both micro- and macroprolactinomas is a dopamine agonist (cabergoline or bromocriptine), which lowers prolactin and reliably shrinks tumor volume.
choice_rationales: Transsphenoidal surgery is reserved for prolactinomas that are resistant to or intolerant of dopamine agonists, or for acute apoplexy—not routine first-line therapy.
Dopamine agonists (cabergoline preferred over bromocriptine) are first-line therapy even for macroprolactinomas, restoring gonadal function and decompressing the optic chiasm medically.
Octreotide and pegvisomant are medical therapies for somatotroph tumors (acromegaly), not lactotroph prolactinomas.
Stalk compression typically raises prolactin modestly (<200 ng/mL); a level of 640 ng/mL with a 2.2 cm mass indicates an autonomous macroprolactinoma requiring active therapy.

Homogeneous solid appearance expanding the bony sella turcica
Upward elevation toward the optic chiasm consistent with a macroadenoma

questions.stem: Under the WHO 2022 PitNET classification, immunohistochemical staining for lineage-restricted transcription factors assigns tumors to three major families. Which transcription-factor-to-hormone pairing is completely accurate?
options: PIT1: GH, ACTH | TPIT: FSH, LH | SF1: PRL, TSH
PIT1: ACTH, MSH | TPIT: TSH, GH | SF1: PRL, oxytocin
PIT1: FSH, LH | TPIT: GH, PRL | SF1: ACTH, TSH

questions.explanation: Step 1. Modern PitNET pathology classifies anterior pituitary tumors by nuclear transcription factors because H&E cannot distinguish lineages. Step 2. PIT1 governs somatotrophs (GH), lactotrophs (PRL), and thyrotrophs (TSH); TPIT governs corticotrophs (ACTH); and SF1 governs gonadotrophs (FSH/LH).
choice_rationales: ACTH belongs to the TPIT lineage and TSH belongs to the PIT1 lineage, not SF1.
ACTH is driven by TPIT rather than PIT1, and oxytocin is a posterior pituitary hypothalamic hormone rather than an SF1 anterior pituitary lineage.
This scrambles all three lineages: SF1—not PIT1—drives gonadotrophs (FSH/LH), and TPIT drives corticotrophs (ACTH).
PIT1 (GH/PRL/TSH), TPIT (ACTH), and SF1 (FSH/LH) are the exact three canonical WHO anterior pituitary lineage transcription factors.

The anterior pituitary has substantial functional reserve, so clinically apparent hypopituitarism usually requires >75% gland loss, and hormone axes typically fail in the sequence GH → FSH/LH → TSH → ACTH → PRL. Step 2. Because GH/IGF-1 stimulates balanced longitudinal growth across the axial and appendicular skeleton, childhood GH deficiency produces proportionate short stature—unlike disproportionate achondroplasia.
choice_rationales: Both statements accurately summarize the >75% reserve threshold, the classic GH → gonadotropin → TSH → ACTH → PRL failure order, and proportionate short stature in GH deficiency.
Neither statement is false; both reflect core E5 hypopituitarism principles.
Statement 2 is also true because pituitary dwarfism preserves normal body proportions, whereas achondroplasia causes rhizomelic limb shortening.
Statement 1 is also true because GH and gonadotropins are the most sensitive anterior axes to progressive compression or destruction.

questions.tested_concept: Water deprivation and desmopressin test distinguishing primary polydipsia, central DI, and nephrogenic DI
questions.stem: A patient with polyuria (>3 L/day) undergoes a formal water deprivation test followed by desmopressin (DDAVP) administration. Which of the following statements about interpreting this test is INCORRECT?
options: In primary polydipsia, water deprivation alone concentrates the urine normally because endogenous ADH and renal V₂ receptors are intact
In complete nephrogenic DI, desmopressin raises urine osmolality >50% because it bypasses renal V₂ receptor resistance
In complete nephrogenic DI, urine remains dilute during water deprivation and fails to concentrate after desmopressin
In complete central DI, urine remains dilute during water deprivation but concentrates markedly after desmopressin
questions.explanation: Step 1. Water deprivation tests endogenous ADH secretion and renal responsiveness: primary polydipsia concentrates urine during deprivation alone, whereas both central and nephrogenic DI fail to concentrate. Step 2. Adding desmopressin separates central DI (urine concentrates markedly because kidneys are intact) from nephrogenic DI (urine stays dilute because renal collecting ducts are unresponsive to ADH/desmopressin)—making the claim that desmopressin bypasses renal V₂ resistance incorrect.
choice_rationales: This statement is correct: patients with primary (psychogenic) polydipsia have an intact neurohypophysis and kidney, so water restriction restores normal urine concentration.
This statement is incorrect: desmopressin is a V₂ receptor agonist and cannot bypass renal V₂ receptor or AQP2 resistance in nephrogenic DI.
This statement is correct: in nephrogenic DI, collecting-duct principal cells are insensitive to both endogenous AVP and exogenous desmopressin.
This statement is correct: exogenous desmopressin replaces missing endogenous ADH in central DI, driving a robust rise in urine osmolality.
